script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Hello, Eastfield Council waste services. How can I help?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: Hi, I missed my recycling collection last Thursday. The bin is still full.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: I'm sorry about that. Can I take your address and postcode?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: It's fourteen Larch Avenue, postcode EF three seven two.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Thank you. We collect paper and card on alternate weeks, and glass and plastic on the other weeks. Which bin is full?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: The blue one, so paper and card.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Then the next collection will be on Tuesday the twenty-second. Please put the bin out by seven in the morning.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: Okay. Can I put cardboard boxes in it too?

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Yes, but the boxes must be flattened. Food-soiled card can't be recycled, so it goes in the general waste bin.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: What if I need a bigger bin?

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Additional bins cost twelve pounds to deliver, and you'd pay a one-off fee of twenty pounds for the bin itself.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: That's more than I expected. I'll manage with the one I have.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: Also, do you collect garden waste?

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Yes, garden waste is collected every other Friday, but only if you have signed up to the garden scheme. There's a separate annual fee for that.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: I haven't signed up. How do I do that?

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: You can sign up on our website, or call this number and we'll send a form to your address.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: And what about batteries and electrical items?

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: They should not go in any household bin. Take them to the recycling centre on Mill Road, which is open every day except Sunday.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining all that.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: You're welcome. Is there anything else I can help you with today?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: No, that's all. Thanks.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Have a good day.

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: Thanks for that. Goodbye.

script.speaker: Council Officer
script.text: Goodbye.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Welcome to the Clockmakers' Gallery. This audio guide covers the four main rooms and takes about forty-five minutes.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: The first room displays early pendulum clocks. The pendulum was introduced in sixteen fifty-six, and it made clocks far more accurate than before.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: In the second room, you'll see the mechanisms. Look closely at the escapement, the part that releases the gears one tooth at a time.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: The third room holds pocket watches. Many of them were made of silver, and the cases were often engraved by hand.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: The final room contains a large astronomical clock. It shows the phases of the moon and the position of the sun, and it is wound once a week.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Please do not touch the exhibits. The gallery is closed on Mondays, and the café on the ground floor is open until half past five.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Guided tours are available on Saturdays at eleven, and booking is required.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: The next room is dedicated to clock faces. Many were painted by hand, using enamel that was fired in a kiln, and some still show traces of the original colours.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Visitors often ask about the restoration work. Our conservators spend several months on each clock, cleaning the movements and replacing worn parts with original materials wherever possible.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Please use the lifts at the back of the building if you need step-free access. The staircase near the entrance is steep and has no handrail on the lower section.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Children under twelve may use the activity table in the reading corner, where they can try simple gears and levers under supervision.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: A reminder that flash photography is not allowed in any room, although photographs without flash are welcome.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: We hope you enjoy your visit. Feedback forms are available at the exit, and your comments help us plan future exhibitions.

title: Preparing for a Graduate Job Interview

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Hello Lucy. You have an interview with the logistics firm next week. How are you feeling about it?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: A bit nervous. I'm not sure how to answer questions about teamwork.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Use the STAR method: situation, task, action and result. Describe a real example from your placement.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: I led a team of four during my placement at the warehouse. We reduced delivery errors.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: That's a strong example. Quantify the result if you can. By how much did errors fall?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: By about a quarter over three months.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Excellent. The firm will also ask why you want to work for them. Have you researched their recent expansion?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Yes, they opened a second distribution centre in the north this year.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Mention that, but don't just repeat the website. Explain what interests you about it.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Should I bring a portfolio?

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Bring a printed copy of your CV and your references, but the portfolio is not needed for this role.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Okay. What time do I need to arrive?

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Arrive fifteen minutes early. The interview is at ten thirty on Wednesday the eleventh, at their Central Park office.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: One more thing: send a thank-you email within twenty-four hours of the interview.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Should I mention anything specific in the email?

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Refer to one point you discussed, and restate your interest. Keep it short, two or three sentences.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: That sounds manageable. What if they ask about my weaknesses?

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Pick a real weakness and describe what you are doing to improve it. Avoid clichés like being a perfectionist.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Okay. I'll practise with a friend tonight.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: Good plan. Good luck, Lucy. Thank you.

script.speaker: Adviser
script.text: And remember to ask two or three questions at the end. It shows that you have researched the company.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Good idea. Thank you.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today's lecture is about Roman roads, which were among the most sophisticated transport networks of the ancient world.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: At their peak, the Roman road system covered more than eighty thousand kilometres. Most roads were built by soldiers, who were trained in surveying and construction.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A typical road had several layers. The base was made of large stones, followed by smaller stones and gravel, and the top surface was paved with flat blocks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Engineers aimed for straight lines wherever possible. Where a river or a hill blocked the way, they built bridges or cut through the rock.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Roads had practical purposes. They allowed armies to move quickly, and they carried messengers, traders and officials across the empire.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Milestones were placed along the roads at regular intervals, showing distances to major cities. Many of these stones survive today.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Some people assume the roads were only for military use. However, the evidence shows that merchants used them heavily, and local communities relied on them for everyday trade.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Next week we'll look at how the roads were maintained, which is a topic that is often overlooked in textbooks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's consider how the roads were surveyed. Surveyors used simple instruments, including a groma, a cross-shaped device with plumb lines, to lay out straight alignments across uneven ground.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Once the route was marked, workers dug a trench and filled it with layers of material. The depth depended on the soil, and in wet areas the foundations were particularly deep.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Drainage was another important feature. Roads were often raised slightly above the surrounding land and fitted with ditches on each side, so that rainwater could run away from the surface.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Some sections still survive well in parts of Europe and North Africa, and their remains show how carefully the builders worked. Archaeologists study wheel ruts and bridge foundations to learn how the roads were used.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Finally, think about the scale of the project. Building such a network required large labour forces, organised supply chains for stone and timber, and strong central administration in Rome. Please read chapter six of the course reader before next week, and bring one question about the maintenance evidence. The reader includes photographs of several surviving milestones, which you should compare with the diagrams we looked at today. Remember the essay on infrastructure is due at the end of the month.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Bring your copy of the reader to the seminar. Attendance is recorded at the start of the session.
